strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving sample efficiency for humanoid whole-body RL, where training cost and sim-to-real robustness are real bottlenecks.

The proposed PvP idea is simple and easy to integrate: align representations from privileged simulator state and a zero-masked/proprioceptive view using a SimSiam-style objective. This simplicity is a strength for adoption.

The manuscript includes a reasonably broad internal study for its chosen setting: two humanoid tasks, comparisons to PPO, VAE, SPR, and SimSiam, plus ablations on SRL update interval, data proportion, and whether SRL is applied to policy or value encoders.

The supplementary material provides useful reproducibility details, including reward terms, observation/state components, network architecture, PPO hyperparameters, and baseline hyperparameter search spaces.
The framework contribution, SRL4Humanoid, could be useful to the robotics/RL community if released as claimed, since unified implementations of SRL baselines for humanoid control are valuable.
weaknesses: The technical novelty is modest. PvP is essentially SimSiam applied to paired privileged and masked simulator states; the paper does not deeply distinguish this from privileged-information distillation, teacher-student learning, or masked reconstruction/representation alignment beyond empirical framing.

The central mechanism is not fully convincing. Because the proprioceptive state is explicitly a subset of the privileged state and the privileged-only components are zero-masked, the contrastive objective may mainly enforce invariance to privileged coordinates rather than transfer missing information. The paper asserts richer privileged information improves proprioceptive representations, but gives little analysis of what information is actually encoded or why collapse/trivial alignment is avoided in this low-dimensional state setting.

The evaluation is limited to one robot platform and two tasks, both apparently non-visual proprioceptive control tasks. For CVPR, the contribution to computer vision or pattern recognition is indirect at best; there is no perception, image/depth input, visual representation learning, or vision benchmark.

Reported results are mostly plotted learning curves without numerical tables, confidence intervals beyond shaded regions, seed counts, statistical tests, or final metric values. This makes it hard to assess effect sizes and robustness of the claimed improvements.

The real-world evaluation is qualitative and weakly documented. The manuscript references screenshots and supporting videos but provides no quantitative hardware metrics, number of trials, success rates, failure cases, command ranges, safety interventions, or comparison to baselines on the real robot.

There are inconsistencies and clarity issues that reduce confidence: the robot/tasks are described as 31 DoF in text, while several figure titles say LimX-Oli-32dof; the method alternates between proprioceptive state o, privileged state s, and zero-masked s without making the exact deployed policy input path fully explicit.

Some claims are overstated relative to the evidence, such as 'guarantee the reliability of real-world deployment' from improved action smoothness in simulation, and 'first unified and modular open-source framework' without visible release details or comparison to existing robotics RL libraries.

Baseline fairness is not fully established. The hyperparameter searches are small and differ by method; PvP may benefit from privileged variables unavailable to several baselines, and the paper does not include stronger privileged-information baselines such as explicit velocity prediction, asymmetric actor-critic variants, teacher-student distillation, or representation distillation losses.

Computational efficiency claims are under-supported. The paper states that SRL adds minimal cost and refers to WandB logs in a compute form, but does not report wall-clock time, GPU memory, throughput, or per-method overhead in the paper.

Reproducibility is only partial: many implementation details are provided, but there is no visible code link in the manuscript text, no seed count, no exact normalization/scoring definition for the normalized curves, and no details on domain randomization or sim-to-real transfer settings.

strengths: The paper targets an important practical problem: improving sample efficiency for humanoid whole-body control, where on-policy RL can be expensive and brittle.

The proposed PvP mechanism is simple and easy to integrate into PPO-style actor-critic training: it applies a SimSiam-like objective between privileged simulator state and a zero-masked/proprioceptive view.
The manuscript includes useful empirical axes beyond a single headline curve, including comparisons to VAE/SPR/SimSiam, update interval, data proportion, and policy-vs-value encoder placement.
The appendix provides some implementation details, including reward terms, observation components, network architecture, and PPO hyperparameters, which partially supports reproducibility.
weaknesses: The novelty is limited. PvP is essentially a SimSiam objective over privileged and masked observations, closely related to privileged-information distillation and teacher-student/adaptation ideas common in robot learning. The paper does not clearly separate its contribution from these prior paradigms or from the SimSiam baseline beyond the choice of paired views.

The main empirical evidence is weakly quantified. Most claims rely on normalized learning curves and bar plots without numerical tables, sample-efficiency metrics, final returns, confidence intervals, number of seeds, or statistical tests. This makes the claimed 'significant' improvements hard to assess.

The evaluation scope is narrow: one proprietary humanoid platform, two tasks, flat-terrain velocity tracking and motion imitation. There is no evaluation on public humanoid benchmarks or other robots, so the claimed broad applicability of PvP is not well supported.

Important baselines are missing or underdeveloped. The paper cites humanoid SRL/world-model and privileged-information methods but compares only against generic VAE, SPR, and SimSiam variants. Stronger robot-learning baselines such as teacher-student privileged distillation, adaptation modules, PIM-style methods, or reconstruction of specific privileged quantities would be more informative.

The real-world evaluation is largely anecdotal. The manuscript refers to screenshots and supporting videos, but reports no quantitative real-robot metrics such as tracking error, success rate, fall rate, deployment duration, commanded velocity coverage, or comparison to PPO/baselines on hardware.

Several technical claims are overstated. For example, Figure 6 is used to claim PvP can 'guarantee the reliability of real-world deployment,' but the evidence is only an action-smoothness reward term in simulation. Computational efficiency is also claimed without reporting wall-clock time, GPU utilization, or overhead numbers.

The method description leaves conceptual ambiguity: aligning representations of privileged state and zero-masked state may encourage invariance to privileged-only information, yet the paper claims it lets the policy access privileged information. The mechanism by which this improves deployable proprioceptive policies is not analyzed convincingly.

Reproducibility is incomplete despite the SRL4Humanoid claim. The manuscript calls the framework open-source but does not provide an accessible code link in the reviewed text, and the WandB logs are said to be in the compute reporting form rather than reported in the paper.

There are presentation and consistency issues that reduce confidence: figures label tasks as '32dof' while the text and robot specification say 31 DoF, the prose contains repeated typos such as 'proproceptive,' and several figures are difficult to interpret because axes are normalized and not tied to concrete reward values.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving sample efficiency for RL-based humanoid whole-body control, where training cost and sim-to-real reliability are real bottlenecks.

The proposed PvP method is simple and technically plausible: using a SimSiam-style objective between privileged simulator state and its proprioceptive/masked counterpart is a clean way to inject privileged information into a deployable policy representation without requiring hand-crafted augmentations at test time.

The experimental study is broader than a single learning curve. It evaluates two meaningful humanoid tasks, velocity tracking and motion imitation, compares against PPO plus VAE, SPR, and SimSiam SRL baselines, and includes ablations on update interval, data proportion, and whether SRL is applied to the policy or value encoder.

The SRL4Humanoid framework is potentially useful to the community. A unified modular implementation of SRL methods for humanoid learning would improve reproducibility and make the paper more than just one algorithmic variant.

The results consistently favor PvP in the presented plots: it improves learning speed and final normalized score, improves action smoothness for velocity tracking, and improves multiple motion imitation KPIs.
The manuscript is generally clear, with a straightforward method section, explicit loss definition, task descriptions, reward terms, network architecture, and PPO hyperparameters in the supplement.
weaknesses: The empirical evidence is convincing in trend but not as rigorous as it could be. Most results are shown as normalized plots without numeric tables, raw returns, seed counts, confidence intervals, or statistical tests, which makes it hard to judge effect sizes and robustness precisely.

Real-world evaluation is mostly qualitative. The paper shows robot deployment and refers to supporting videos, but does not provide quantitative real-robot metrics, failure rates, number of trials, command distributions, safety interventions, or sim-to-real gap analysis.

The benchmark breadth is limited to one humanoid platform and two tasks on relatively constrained settings. This is still valuable, but the claim of broad applicability across humanoid WBC would be stronger with additional robots, terrains, disturbances, or more diverse motion sets.

The method’s novelty is moderate rather than high. PvP is an elegant combination of privileged learning and SimSiam-style contrastive representation learning, but it is conceptually close to privileged distillation / auxiliary privileged prediction ideas; the paper could better distinguish what is fundamentally new beyond the choice of contrastive loss and masking construction.

Some experimental details are underspecified or slightly inconsistent. The main text alternates between 31-DoF and figure labels saying 32-DoF, and it is unclear how many random seeds were used, how evaluation episodes were sampled, and whether hyperparameter tuning budget was equal across baselines.

The computational efficiency claim is weakly supported in the manuscript itself. The paper says SRL has minimal overhead and logs are attached to the CRF, but does not report wall-clock time, GPU memory, throughput, or overhead per method in the paper.

The real contribution of SRL4Humanoid depends heavily on code release quality, but the manuscript does not provide enough concrete information about API design, supported environments, documentation, or reproducibility package status to fully assess that claim.

Because the work is primarily robotics/RL rather than computer vision, its fit to CVPR depends on the venue’s appetite for embodied learning papers. The paper does not include visual perception inputs; its connection to computer vision is indirect through representation learning and embodied intelligence.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving sample efficiency for RL-based humanoid whole-body control under partial observability. The proposed proprioceptive-privileged contrastive objective is simple, easy to integrate with PPO, and well motivated by the gap between simulator-only privileged state and deployable proprioceptive observations.

The empirical section covers several relevant comparisons: vanilla PPO, VAE, SPR, SimSiam, teacher-student distillation in the appendix, different SRL update intervals, different data proportions, policy vs value encoder placement, and additional appendix tasks including rough terrain and a different humanoid platform.

The reported learning curves consistently suggest that PvP improves convergence speed and often final normalized return, especially on the main velocity tracking task and in the appendix rough-terrain/G1 results.
The SRL4Humanoid framework, if released as described, could be useful to the robotics/RL community because it provides a unified implementation of multiple SRL objectives for humanoid control.

The paper is generally readable, with clear high-level diagrams and enough implementation detail in the appendix to understand the policy/value architectures, PPO hyperparameters, reward terms, and state components.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. PvP is essentially a SimSiam-style alignment between a privileged-state view and a masked deployable-state view. This is a sensible design, but it is close in spirit to privileged learning, teacher-student/asymmetric actor-critic methods, and representation distillation; the paper does not sharply establish what is technically new beyond this particular pairing.

The evidence is overly reliant on plotted normalized learning curves. The paper does not provide tabulated final returns, sample-efficiency metrics, confidence intervals, number of seeds, statistical tests, or absolute task metrics for the main claims, making it difficult to judge the magnitude and reliability of the reported gains.

Real-world validation is weakly documented. The manuscript shows images and refers to supplementary videos, but gives no quantitative real-robot results such as tracking error, fall/success rate, duration, command coverage, disturbance robustness, or comparison against baselines on hardware. Claims about deployment reliability are therefore not fully supported.

The benchmark breadth is limited for a CVPR-level claim of generality: the main paper evaluates two tasks on one robot, both in proprioceptive humanoid control rather than vision-centric perception. Appendix additions help, but the core contribution remains mostly within robot RL rather than computer vision/pattern recognition.

Some experimental comparisons are potentially unfair or underexplained. Baseline SRL methods depend heavily on augmentation choices and loss weights, but the hyperparameter search is described only coarsely. The teacher-student baseline appears unusually poor in the appendix, and more detail is needed to verify it is a strong implementation.

Important reproducibility details are missing or hard to verify from the manuscript alone, including seed count, normalization procedure for scores, exact privileged/proprioceptive alignment at inference, domain randomization settings, simulator versions, control frequency, real-robot safety filters, and compute-time comparisons beyond a qualitative statement about WandB/CRF logs.

Several claims are stronger than the evidence warrants, e.g. that PvP 'guarantees' real-world deployment reliability or 'significantly' improves performance, despite limited quantitative support and no formal significance analysis.

Presentation issues reduce clarity in places: some formulas and algorithm references are inconsistent, several figures are small and lack exact values, and the real-world/code repository footnote is not visible in the extracted manuscript text. These are fixable but currently make independent assessment harder.

strengths: The paper addresses an important practical problem: improving sample efficiency for humanoid whole-body RL under partial observability, where privileged simulation state is available during training but not deployment.

The proposed PvP loss is simple and easy to integrate: it adapts a SimSiam-style objective to align representations from privileged-state and zero-masked/proprioceptive inputs, which is a reasonable training-time auxiliary signal.

The experiments include two relevant humanoid tasks, velocity tracking and motion imitation, and compare against PPO plus several SRL auxiliaries. The appendices provide useful implementation details such as reward terms, state components, network architecture, and PPO hyperparameters.
The SRL4Humanoid framework, if actually released with usable code, could be useful infrastructure for comparing SRL methods in humanoid robot learning.

The paper includes some ablations on SRL update interval, data proportion, encoder placement, teacher-student distillation, and additional rough-terrain / Unitree-G1 settings, which helps support the claim that the method is not purely a one-task artifact.
weaknesses: The core methodological novelty is limited. PvP is essentially SimSiam applied to two views formed by privileged-state input and zero-masked proprioceptive input. The idea of using privileged information to shape deployable representations is closely related to teacher-student learning, asymmetric actor-critic training, privileged distillation, and adaptation modules; the paper does not convincingly establish what is technically new beyond this straightforward combination.

The experimental evidence is too qualitative for the strength of the claims. Most results are plotted as normalized learning curves without raw returns, final metrics, confidence intervals beyond shaded standard deviations, seed counts, statistical tests, or tabulated quantitative comparisons. This makes it hard to assess effect size, stability, and whether improvements are practically meaningful.

The real-world evaluation is especially weak. The manuscript mainly points to Figure 1 and supplementary videos, with no quantitative hardware metrics, number of trials, failure rates, tracking errors, safety interventions, or comparison against baselines on the robot. Thus claims about real-world deployment reliability are not adequately supported.

The baseline set is not fully convincing. The main comparisons are generic SRL auxiliaries such as VAE, SPR, and SimSiam, while stronger and more directly relevant privileged-learning, teacher-student, adaptation, recurrent, or humanoid-control baselines are either absent or relegated to limited appendix plots. The TSD discussion is also somewhat one-sided and lacks enough setup detail to judge fairness.

Several claims are overstated. For example, the paper says PvP can guarantee real-world deployment reliability based on smoother action penalties in simulation, which is not justified. It also claims broad task versatility, but the main evaluation is only two tasks on one primary robot, with additional settings only in the appendix.

Important reproducibility details are missing or underspecified despite some useful appendix material. The paper does not clearly report random seeds, evaluation protocol, exact normalization of scores, domain randomization settings, sim-to-real pipeline, hardware trial protocol, or full compute/runtime numbers beyond saying experiments ran on an RTX4090 and WandB logs were attached to a CRF.

The technical formulation has ambiguities. The paper assumes the proprioceptive state is a subset of the privileged state, but the listed state definitions include stacked proprioceptive histories and task-specific privileged components that make the exact alignment and zero-masking procedure unclear. The policy encoder input dimensionality and how deployment-time padded inputs are handled should be specified more rigorously.

The analysis of why PvP works remains shallow. The paper does not inspect learned representations, quantify representation alignment, isolate the contribution of privileged variables, compare against direct privileged prediction/regression losses, or explain when the contrastive objective may hurt. The update-interval and data-proportion studies are useful but mostly descriptive.

The writing is generally understandable, but it often uses broad promotional language instead of precise evidence. Several sections would benefit from clearer distinctions between demonstrated results, plausible explanations, and future aspirations.

strengths: The paper targets an important problem: improving sample efficiency and robustness for humanoid whole-body control, where RL training cost and sim-to-real reliability are major practical bottlenecks.

The proposed PvP objective is simple and technically plausible: it aligns representations from privileged simulator state and zero-masked/proprioceptive state using a SimSiam-style contrastive loss, giving the policy encoder a way to benefit from privileged information during training without requiring privileged inputs at deployment.

The SRL4Humanoid framework contribution is useful. The paper integrates PPO with several representative SRL families, including VAE, SPR, SimSiam, and PvP, and studies where and how SRL losses should be applied in humanoid WBC.

The experiments are broader than a minimal proof of concept: the main evaluation covers velocity tracking and motion imitation on LimX Oli, with additional appendix experiments on rough terrain and a different Unitree G1 platform.

The ablations are informative. The paper studies SRL update interval, training data proportion, applying SRL to policy versus value encoders, teacher-student distillation comparisons, and the PvP loss weight, which supports the central design choices.

The work includes practical deployment evidence via Sim2Sim and real-robot demonstrations, which is valuable for humanoid control papers and strengthens the case that the method is not only a simulation artifact.
weaknesses: The novelty is moderate. PvP is essentially a SimSiam-style alignment between privileged and masked/proprioceptive views, and it is closely related in spirit to privileged learning, asymmetric actor-critic training, teacher-student distillation, and representation alignment. The paper could more sharply distinguish the conceptual contribution from these lines.

Most quantitative results are shown as normalized learning curves without exact numerical tables for final performance, sample-efficiency gains, wall-clock costs, or real-world success metrics. This makes it harder to assess the magnitude and consistency of the claimed improvements.

The number of random seeds is not clearly stated, despite shaded mean/std regions. For RL humanoid control, variance can be substantial, so missing seed counts and statistical significance weaken the evidential strength.

The real-world evaluation is mainly qualitative. The paper shows robot deployment and refers to videos, but does not report quantitative hardware metrics such as tracking error, fall rate, energy/action smoothness on hardware, or number of successful trials.

The computational efficiency claim is under-supported in the manuscript. Section 5.2.5 states that SRL has minimal overhead and refers to WandB logs/CRF, but does not provide a clear table of training time, memory, or overhead for each method.

Some implementation details remain underspecified for reproduction, including the exact SRL update schedule used in the final comparisons, seed count, normalization of scores, domain randomization settings, and complete real-world deployment protocol.

The paper is framed for humanoid robotics rather than core computer vision or pattern recognition. While embodied AI is relevant to CVPR, the visual/perceptual component is limited; the contribution is primarily in RL representation learning for robot proprioception.
